problem.title: Why do point-in-time scanners miss security drift?
problem.p1: Your attack surface shifts every week: dozens of SaaS tools tied to company data, coding agents opening pull requests, years of accumulated roles and configs. Each standalone tool sees only its narrow slice.
problem.p2: An annual audit or quarterly scan captures a snapshot that drifts the next morning. A temporary role widened for a release, a dependency bump, an open storage bucket: CTOs and CISOs need a continuous loop.
problem.p3: Exposed secrets and legacy runtimes stay the easiest open doors. We analyzed those exact patterns in <link>Black October: what it means for AI agents</link>.

whatFor.q: What does Quivr do for me, in plain words?
whatFor.a: It keeps every article, email and post, even when a service goes down, and keeps the earlier version when one is corrected. It lets you search by meaning, not just keywords, and shows the exact passage. And it tells your app when a new article matches a topic you described, with the reason it matched.

underTheHood.a: A Go engine, one binary for the API, the worker and migrations, on PostgreSQL, S3-compatible storage and Temporal. Search runs on Weaviate, by keyword and by vector, with multilingual E5 embeddings. It exposes an HTTP API (v0), signed webhooks, a change feed (polling or SSE) and MCP for AI agents.

v1.a: Quivr V2 replaced the V1 code base on the main branch. V1 is preserved at the v1-final tag, the last commit of Quivr V1, so you can still read, fork or run it from there.

license.a: MIT. It is free to use, modify and self-host. Some plugins rely on libraries with their own license, such as pypdf (BSD-3-Clause) for the PDF plugin.

production.q: Can I use Quivr V2 in production?
production.a: Not yet. Quivr V2 is at the evaluation stage and its API is v0, which may change without notice. Try it on your machine with the Quickstart, and talk to us if you want to plan a production rollout.

selfHost.a: Yes. Quivr runs on servers you control, next to your application: one machine with Docker Compose to evaluate it, or a deployment with separate workers and a dedicated vector host. By default, Quivr itself sends document text nowhere outside your installation.

support.a: For questions and bugs, use the issues and discussions of the GitHub repository. For business plugins, planning a production rollout, or hosting that works to HDS requirements for health data, The Vibe Company can help as a service: book a call.

items.title: Audience measurement with PostHog
paragraphs: On the production site only, the PostHog library records page views (the page address, query string included, for instance the text of a search in the resources), page leaves, the clicks and interactions it captures automatically, click and scroll positions for heatmaps, page performance measurements (Web Vitals) and JavaScript errors. On top of that come the events we named ourselves: clicks on our booking, contact and navigation buttons, opening the mobile menu, a search in the resources (query length and word count only), expanding or copying a skill prompt, games of the homepage mini-game, with their score and, when a record falls, the previous record.

PostHog adds technical details: browser, operating system, screen size, referring page, campaign parameters (utm_*) and ad click identifiers found in the address (gclid, fbclid, msclkid, li_fat_id, ttclid…).

The data goes through /ingest, a relay on our own domain, then on to PostHog, in its United States region. Measurement is cookieless: PostHog stores nothing in your browser, no cookie, no localStorage, no sessionStorage. Each visit is measured without a persistent identifier: PostHog draws a random identifier that lives in memory only, for as long as you browse the site in that tab, and is gone as soon as you reload or close the page. From one visit to the next, the same person is not recognized. The PostHog project setting that anonymizes IP addresses isn’t turned on, so the IP address sent with events isn’t masked by that setting, and by default PostHog derives an approximate location from it (country, region, city, approximate coordinates, time zone) and adds it to the events. The site never calls PostHog’s identify function and creates no person profile. Your visits aren’t tied to your name or email.
Session recording (replay) is turned off in the PostHog project, and surveys are not enabled.

items.title: Booking with cal.com
paragraphs: The booking buttons are plain links to cal.com. The site embeds no cal.com widget and loads nothing from cal.com until you click. The click itself is counted in PostHog.
On cal.com, you enter your name, your email and the details of the meeting. Cal.com processes them under its own privacy policy, and we receive them to prepare the call.

When a meeting is booked, cal.com notifies our server. We then record a single PostHog event, “booking_completed”, with the booking identifier (failing that, a salted hash of the email, never the email itself), the start time, the duration and any campaign parameters. Your name, your email and the content of the booking are not sent to PostHog.

items.title: Email
paragraphs: If you write to us, we receive your email address, your name if it appears and the content of your message. They are used to answer you and keep track of the conversation.

items.title: Hosting on Vercel
paragraphs: The site is hosted by Vercel. Like any host, Vercel processes the technical data of each request (IP address, browser, requested page, date and time) to serve pages and protect the service. Traffic to the site is encrypted over HTTPS. Pages are served from Vercel’s network, close to the visitor. The site’s server functions, such as receiving cal.com notifications, run in Washington, D.C., United States (region iad1).

When you open an address that doesn’t specify a language, such as /contact, the site reads the country Vercel derives from your IP address to choose between French and English. The site does not store that country.
Vercel Web Analytics and Speed Insights are not installed. Fonts are served from our own domain: no request goes to Google Fonts.

paragraphs: The GDPR and the French Data Protection Act give you several rights over your data. You can access it, have it corrected or erased, object to its processing or ask for it to be restricted. You can also receive the data you gave us in a reusable format (portability). There are only a few, none of them asks for an account or an email, and the first one is live: it tests your website and tells you whether ChatGPT, Claude or Perplexity can find it and read it. intro.title: What you will find here
intro.p1: Every tool on this page is built by The Vibe Company, an <agencyLink>AI agency in Paris</agencyLink>. The rule is the same for all of them: free, no sign-up, and simple enough to give you a result straight away.
intro.p2: The collection is small. Today it is one tool, a checker that tells you whether your website is ready for AI agents. You give it your site's address and it hands back a score and a list of what to fix.

agentReady.title: The first tool: is your website ready for AI agents?
agentReady.p1: Your customers increasingly ask ChatGPT, Claude or Perplexity to compare options, summarize a page or book something for them. To answer, those assistants go and visit the websites involved. If they cannot read yours, they cite your competitors.
agentReady.p2: We made the checker for whoever owns that problem in a small or mid-size company, whether they sit in marketing or in tech. You enter your website's address and the tool tests the root of the site. It runs 16 checks on your public pages: the home page, robots.txt, the sitemap, llms.txt and the standard files of agent protocols. The result comes back in under 30 seconds.
agentReady.p3: You leave with a score out of 100, a level from 0 to 5 for each category and an explanation in plain language. Every point to fix comes with instructions you can paste into a coding agent such as Claude Code, Cursor or Codex.
agentReady.discovery: The first category, Discoverability, asks the basic question: can agents find your pages? robots.txt is your site's house rules, the file search engines and AI assistants read before anything else. The sitemap gives them all your pages in a single request. And llms.txt sums up who you are and where your key pages live.
agentReady.content: The Content category picks up once they have arrived: can they read you without a browser? Many agents do not run JavaScript. If your home page only shows its text after a script has run, they see an empty page. The checker also looks at whether your site can serve its pages as Markdown, which agents prefer to HTML.
agentReady.bots: The AI crawlers category checks whether you let these visitors in, and on what terms. There is what your robots.txt says to the main AI crawlers, and there is what really happens. A crawler asking for your home page should get it, with no block and no "are you human?" challenge. A blocked crawler does not cite your site in its answers.
agentReady.protocols: Agent protocols, the last scored category, mostly matters for online services. It looks for the files that tell an agent it can take action on your site, such as the card of an <mcpLink>MCP server</mcpLink>. Checks that do not apply to your site do not count toward the score.
agentReady.commerce: A fifth section, Commerce, reports whether an agent can pay you through the x402 protocol. That one is still emerging, so it is shown for information and stays outside the score.

llms.title: What is llms.txt, and does your site need one?
llms.p1: llms.txt is a summary of your website written for AI models. It is a Markdown file that lives at /llms.txt and is served as text/plain or text/markdown.
llms.p2: There is not much in it. It opens with a heading in the form "# Name of your company", followed by a one-line presentation and a list of your important pages with their links.
llms.p3: A sitemap lists every page you have. llms.txt says in a few lines who you are and which pages to read first, which makes it the simplest way in for an assistant.
llms.p4: The agent-ready checker looks for this file on your site. It is an llms.txt checker, not a generator. If the file is missing, the report explains what to put in it and gives you instructions to paste into your coding agent.

score.title: How to read your score, and what to fix first
score.p1: The score out of 100 combines the four scored categories. Checks do not all weigh the same. The essentials count for more: readable content, real AI crawler access, robots.txt and the sitemap. Each category also gets its own level, from 0 to 5.
score.p2: Those weights give you the order of work. Start by making sure AI crawlers get in and that your text is present in the HTML. Then tidy up robots.txt and the sitemap, and add an llms.txt. Agent protocols come later, if you run an online service.
score.p3: The basic fixes do not call for a technical team. Each point is explained simply, and a copy button prepares the instructions for your coding agent. They often take less than a day.

free.q: Are these AI tools really free?
free.a: Yes. They are free and work with no sign-up: no account to create, no email to leave.

ready.q: What does "ready for AI agents" mean?
ready.a: It means AI assistants and agents can find, read and understand your website with no effort: a clear robots.txt, a sitemap, an llms.txt summary, text present in the HTML and open access for AI crawlers. For an online service it also covers protocols like MCP, so an agent can take action.

llms.q: Does the tool generate my llms.txt file?
llms.a: No, it checks that the file is there. If it is missing, the report describes what it should contain (a heading, a one-line presentation, a list of your important pages) and provides instructions to paste into a coding agent.

data.q: What does the test do on my site, and what do you keep?
data.a: The test only reads public pages, as a visitor would, with no login and no form. The report stays in memory for a few minutes so the same test is not run twice, then it is forgotten. We only measure the tested domain name and the score, to improve the tool.

dev.q: I have no developer. Can I fix things myself?
dev.a: Often, yes. Every point comes with a simple explanation and the fix to apply, and the instructions paste straight into Claude Code, Cursor or Codex. The basic fixes often take less than a day.

robots_txt.name: robots.txt file
robots_txt.explain: robots.txt is your website's house rules for bots. Search engines and AI assistants read it first to learn where they may go.
robots_txt.fix: Serve a text file at /robots.txt with status 200 and type text/plain, holding at least one User-agent group (for example "User-agent: *" followed by "Allow: /").

sitemap.name: Sitemap
sitemap.explain: A sitemap lists all your pages. An agent finds in a single request what it would otherwise discover link by link, and sees what changed recently.
sitemap.fix: Publish a sitemap.xml served as XML (most CMSs generate one for you) and declare its full address in robots.txt with a line like "Sitemap: https://www.yourcompany.com/sitemap.xml".

link_headers.name: Link headers
link_headers.explain: An HTTP Link header on the home page tells agents, before they even read the page, where to find your useful resources: a summary for AI, a Markdown version, your API description.
link_headers.fix: Add an HTTP Link header to the home page response with a describedby, service-desc, api-catalog or alternate relation, for example: Link: </llms.txt>; rel="describedby".

llms_txt.name: llms.txt file
llms_txt.explain: llms.txt is a summary of your website written for AI models: who you are, your key pages and their links. It is the simplest way in for an assistant.
llms_txt.fix: Publish a Markdown file at /llms.txt, served as text/plain or text/markdown, that starts with a "# Your company name" heading, followed by a one-sentence introduction and the list of your important pages.

markdown_negotiation.name: Markdown version of pages
markdown_negotiation.explain: Agents prefer Markdown to HTML: less noise, lower cost. When they ask for it, your site can serve them the same page as clean text.
markdown_negotiation.fix: When a request for the home page sends Accept: text/markdown, answer 200 with Content-Type: text/markdown and the page content in Markdown. Add Vary: Accept so caches keep both versions.

raw_html_content.name: Content readable without JavaScript
raw_html_content.explain: Many agents do not run JavaScript. If your home page only shows its text once a script has run, they see an empty page.
raw_html_content.fix: Render the page on the server (server rendering or static pages) so the initial HTML holds a non-empty H1 heading and at least a few sentences of visible text (200 characters or more).

robots_ai_rules.name: Rules for AI crawlers
robots_ai_rules.explain: Does your robots.txt allow the main AI crawlers: GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ClaudeBot, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot and Google-Extended? A blocked crawler does not cite your site in its answers.
robots_ai_rules.fix: In robots.txt, allow these crawlers: either with a "User-agent: *" group that does not disallow the root, or with a dedicated group for each one with "Allow: /". Remove the Disallow lines aimed at them if you want to appear in their answers.

content_signal.name: Content usage signal
content_signal.explain: The Content-Signal directive, placed in robots.txt, states how your content may be used: search, AI assistant answers, model training.
content_signal.fix: Add a line to robots.txt such as "Content-Signal: search=yes, ai-input=yes, ai-train=no", adapted to your choices.

ai_bot_access.name: Real AI crawler access
ai_bot_access.explain: Beyond the rules, we check that an AI crawler visiting your home page actually gets it, with no block and no "are you human?" challenge page.
ai_bot_access.fix: In your firewall, CDN or bot protection, let through the AI crawlers you want to welcome (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot…) so they get the page with status 200, without a challenge or captcha.

mcp_server_card.name: MCP server card
mcp_server_card.explain: MCP is the protocol that lets AI assistants use tools. A card published on your site tells them an MCP server exists and how to connect to it. Useful if you offer a service or data.
mcp_server_card.fix: If you run an MCP server, publish its JSON description at /.well-known/mcp.json (or /.well-known/mcp/server-card.json), served as application/json. Otherwise, this can wait.

a2a_agent_card.name: A2A agent card
a2a_agent_card.explain: A2A lets agents talk to each other. An agent card describes what your agent can do and how to reach it.
a2a_agent_card.fix: If you expose an agent, publish its JSON card at /.well-known/agent-card.json, served as application/json, following the A2A specification. Otherwise, this can wait.

agent_skills.name: Agent skills index
agent_skills.explain: Skills are reusable instructions for agents. An index published on your site lets agents discover the ones you offer.
agent_skills.fix: Publish a JSON index of your skills at /.well-known/agent-skills/index.json, served as application/json. Otherwise, this can wait.

oauth_discovery.name: OAuth discovery
oauth_discovery.explain: If your service has user accounts, an agent needs to know how to get authorization. The OAuth or OpenID discovery document gives it the right addresses.
oauth_discovery.fix: Publish your authorization server metadata at /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server or /.well-known/openid-configuration, as application/json. Most identity providers do this for you.

oauth_protected_resource.name: OAuth protected resource
oauth_protected_resource.explain: This document tells an agent which authorization server protects your API, so it knows where to ask for access.
oauth_protected_resource.fix: Publish /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource as application/json, with at least the resource field and the authorization_servers list (RFC 9728).

api_catalog.name: API catalog
api_catalog.explain: An API catalog lists your public APIs and their documentation at a standard address, so an agent finds them without searching.
api_catalog.fix: Publish /.well-known/api-catalog as application/linkset+json, with a link to each API's description (OpenAPI for example), following RFC 9727.

x402.name: Agent payments (x402)
x402.explain: The x402 protocol lets an agent pay for content or a service directly over HTTP. It is still emerging: we flag it for information, with no effect on the score.
x402.fix: Nothing required. If you sell pay-per-use access (API, data), x402 lets you answer 402 with the payment terms.

checksSection.lede: Four scored categories, and a fifth for information. The heaviest checks are the ones that matter for every website: being found, being read, letting crawlers in.

what.q: What does an agent-ready website mean?
what.a: It is a website that AI assistants and agents can find, read and understand with no effort: a clear robots.txt, a sitemap, an llms.txt summary, text present in the HTML and open access for AI crawlers. For online services it also covers protocols like MCP, so an agent can take action.

why.q: Why does it matter for a small business?
why.a: Your customers increasingly ask ChatGPT, Claude or Perplexity to compare, summarize or book for them. If these assistants cannot read your website, they cite your competitors. The basic fixes often take less than a day.

data.q: What does the test do on my site, and do you keep my data?
data.a: The test only reads public pages, as a visitor would, with no login and no form. The report stays in memory for a few minutes so the same test is not run twice, then it is forgotten. No account, no email: we only measure the tested domain name and the score, to improve the tool.

score.a: Each check has a weight, higher for the essentials: readable content, AI crawler access, robots.txt and sitemap. A category gets the share of points earned, and a level from 0 to 5. The overall score combines the four scored categories. Checks that do not apply and x402 commerce do not count.

fix.q: I have no developer: how do I fix it?
fix.a: Every point to fix comes with a simple explanation and the fix to apply. The copy button prepares instructions to paste into a coding agent like Claude Code, Cursor or Codex. And if you would rather have help, you can book 30 minutes with us from the report.
